idiom_name: sequence.lazy.map { }.filter { } forced by for-in or Array(...)
implementation_notes: Swift's standard library ships the pattern under the name laziness: LazySequenceProtocol implements normally-eager operations (map, filter, compactMap, prefix) as wrapper types that store the closure and the base sequence and compute elements on demand, .lazy on any Sequence gives explicit permission to defer, and the result is itself lazy so further transformations keep composing. The sink is whatever consumes the result - for-in, first(where:), reduce, or an Array(...) initialisation that materialises deliberately. What replaces the classic structure: closure-storing wrapper types (LazyMapSequence, LazyFilterSequence) plus the standard library's default implementations replace a reducing-function transformer, and no accumulator protocol appears anywhere in the chain; the classic transducer value is justified only when one transformation must feed a non-Sequence sink (a Combine publisher, an AsyncSequence, a callback API) or be stored as a single erased type.
pitfalls: Lazy wrappers recompute on every traversal: iterating the same lazy sequence twice runs the closures twice, and side effects run at consumption time rather than at chain construction.
The eager/lazy mismatch is silent: assigning a lazy result to an Array-typed API or passing it to an eager function materialises everything and hangs on infinite sequences.
Lazy wrappers capture the base sequence and the closure for as long as the pipeline is stored, so a long-lived lazy value retains its source (and any captured self).

variants.name: AsyncSequence operators (Swift concurrency)
variants.implementation_notes: Under Swift concurrency the same transformation vocabulary exists for asynchronous sources: AsyncSequence's map/compactMap/filter are transformations returning another sequence (AsyncMapSequence, AsyncFilterSequence) and the sink is a for await loop or a terminal operator such as reduce/first(where:) on an async sequence. Because the transformations do not eagerly await the next element, the caller decides when work starts, and cancellation propagates through the enclosing task. What replaces the classic structure: the sequence itself is the transformation pipeline and the iterator protocol supplies pull, backpressure and cancellation, so no transducer protocol is needed. Combine is the reactive counterpart - publishers compose with map/filter and terminate in sink/assign - and is the better fit when backpressure, multicast or scheduler semantics matter; the classic transducer object is justified only when one pipeline must be shared between the synchronous and asynchronous worlds.
pitfalls: An AsyncSequence is single-pass by default: most sequences can be iterated once only, so re-iterating an AsyncStream (or a mapped form of one) yields nothing after the first pass.
Stage closures must be @Sendable: capturing non-Sendable state in a transformation is a compile error or a data race under strict concurrency, and blocking work inside an operator blocks the task.
Cancellation and backpressure belong to the source's iterator, not to the operators - a stage cannot slow a producer unless the source implements the buffering policy (e.g. AsyncStream's).
